claims.text: Search known sources first, including springs, streams, rivers, lakes, and maintained water points.
Because water moves downhill, look in valleys, drainage channels, gullies, and low points between hills.
Greener or denser vegetation may indicate moisture, but it does not guarantee safe drinking water.
Animal tracks, repeated trails, and bird activity may indicate water direction, but they do not establish water safety.
Adapt the search to the environment and reduce exposure or exertion before continuing when conditions make the search hazardous.
Assess a found water source for visible or detectable contamination before collecting it.
Avoid water with a fuel smell, chemical odor, oily appearance, industrial pollution, or dead animals nearby.
Be cautious with water showing green surface scum, a paint-like appearance, unusual foam, or a strong odor.
Boiling does not remove all toxins produced by harmful algal blooms.
Use hygienic handling and thorough cooking to reduce foodborne illness risk from wild game.
Keep meat and tools clean, and keep raw meat separate from cooked and ready-to-eat food.
Do not rely only on appearance, smell, or texture because wild game can contain parasites and pathogens.
To roast fish or meat pieces, prepare the food, place it near controlled heat, rotate it regularly, and cook it completely.
To boil meat, plants, or soup, add the food and water, heat thoroughly, and maintain the cooking temperature.
Coal cooking can provide stable heat and better temperature control.
Keep raw meat, waste, and contaminated tools in a dirty area separate from cooked food, clean equipment, and ready-to-eat items.
